name: Net Operating Profit after Tax (NOPAT)
description: Gives the operating profit a company would earn after tax if it had no debt.
notes: The numerator of ROIC and EVA.

name: Return on Invested Capital (ROIC)
description: Divides NOPAT by the capital invested in operations (debt plus equity, less excess cash).
notes: A company creates value when ROIC exceeds its WACC.

name: Economic Value Added (EVA)
description: Subtracts a charge for all the capital used from NOPAT; positive EVA means profit above the cost of capital (Stern Stewart).

name: Market Value Added (MVA)

variables.label: Market value of debt and equity

description: Gives the wealth a company has created for investors: market value minus the capital they put in.
notes: In theory it equals the present value of all future EVA.

name: Cost of Equity (Dividend Growth Model)
description: Estimates the return shareholders require from the dividend yield plus expected dividend growth.
notes: Rearranged Gordon growth model; sensitive to the growth assumption.

name: Cost of Equity with Flotation Costs
description: Gives the cost of newly issued equity, which is higher than that of retained earnings because of issuing costs.
notes: Here 9.42 % against 9.2 % without flotation costs.

name: Cost of Preferred Stock
description: Divides the fixed preferred dividend by the net price received.
notes: No tax adjustment, since preferred dividends are not deductible.

name: Modigliani–Miller Value of a Levered Firm
description: Adds the present value of the perpetual interest tax shield t·D to the value of the unlevered firm (MM 1963).
notes: Ignores costs of financial distress, which limit borrowing in practice.

name: Modigliani–Miller Cost of Equity
description: Gives the cost of equity rising with leverage: r_E = r_U + (r_U − r_D)(1 − t)D/E (MM proposition II with taxes).

name: Adjusted Present Value (APV)
description: Values a project as its all-equity NPV plus the present value of the interest tax shields of permanent debt.
notes: Suits leveraged buyouts and projects whose debt changes over time.

name: Justified (Leading) P/E Ratio
description: Gives the P/E ratio on next year's earnings implied by the Gordon growth model: payout/(r − g).
notes: Multiply by (1 + g) for the trailing P/E.

name: Justified Price-to-Book Ratio
description: Gives the P/B ratio justified by fundamentals: (ROE − g)/(r − g).
notes: A company earning more than its cost of equity deserves to trade above book value.

name: Residual Income
description: Gives profit after charging for the equity capital used: net income minus r times book equity.
notes: Positive residual income means the firm beat its cost of equity.

name: Single-Stage Residual Income Valuation
description: Values a share as book value plus the present value of residual income growing at g.
notes: Gives 50 here, the same as the justified P/B of 2.5 times book.

name: Two-Stage Dividend Discount Model
description: Values a share whose dividends grow fast for n years and then at a stable rate forever.
notes: The second term is the Gordon value at year n, discounted to today.

name: H-Model Share Value
expression: d0 * (1 + gl) / (r - gl) + d0 * h * (gs - gl) / (r - gl)
description: Values a share whose dividend growth declines linearly from a high to a long-run rate over 2H years (Fuller–Hsia 1984).
notes: An approximation that avoids the abrupt switch of the two-stage model.

name: DCF Enterprise Value from Forecast Free Cash Flows
expression: sum(k, 1, len(fc), at(fc, k) / (1 + w)^k) + at(fc, len(fc)) * (1 + g) / ((w - g) * (1 + w)^len(fc))
description: Discounts explicit free-cash-flow forecasts and a Gordon terminal value at the WACC to give enterprise value.
notes: The terminal value usually makes up most of the result; test it with a range of growth rates.

name: Exit-Multiple Terminal Value
description: Values the business at the end of the forecast with a market multiple and discounts it to today.
notes: Compare with the perpetuity-growth terminal value as a cross-check.

name: Merger EPS Accretion/Dilution
description: Compares the combined company's EPS with the acquirer's stand-alone EPS; positive means accretive.
notes: Accretion alone does not prove a deal creates value.

name: Share Exchange Ratio
description: Gives the number of acquirer shares given for each target share in a stock deal.
notes: Here 0.75 acquirer shares per target share.

name: Acquisition Premium
description: Gives how far the offer price exceeds the target's share price before the deal was known.
notes: Typical public takeovers carry premiums of 20–40 %.

name: Depreciation Tax Shield
description: Gives the tax saved because depreciation is deductible.
notes: Accelerated depreciation brings the shield forward and so raises NPV.

name: After-Tax Salvage Value
description: Gives the cash kept when an asset is sold: the price minus tax on the gain over its tax book value.
notes: A sale below book value produces a tax saving instead.

name: Operating Cash Flow (Indirect Method)
description: Converts net income to operating cash flow by adding back non-cash charges and subtracting the growth in working capital.
notes: Other non-cash items (impairments, share-based pay) are added back the same way.

name: Free Cash Flow (Simple)
description: Gives the cash left after the investment needed to keep and grow the business.
notes: The quantity many investors watch most closely.

name: Free Cash Flow Yield
description: Divides free cash flow by market capitalisation, the cash-based counterpart of the earnings yield.
notes: Here 6.5 %.

name: EBITDA (Earnings before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation)
description: Adds depreciation and amortisation back to operating profit (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation).
notes: A rough proxy for operating cash flow, but it ignores capital spending and working capital.

name: Cash Coverage Ratio
description: Divides EBITDA by interest expense, showing how many times cash earnings cover interest.
notes: Complements the interest coverage ratio, which uses EBIT.

name: Working Capital Turnover
description: Measures revenue generated per unit of net working capital.
notes: Very high values can signal too little working capital to support growth.

name: Price-to-Cash-Flow Ratio
description: Divides the share price by operating cash flow per share.
notes: Harder to flatter with accounting choices than the P/E ratio.

name: EV/Sales Multiple
description: Divides enterprise value by revenue; used for companies that are not yet profitable.
notes: Compare only within an industry, since margins differ widely.

name: Dividend Cover
description: Gives how many times earnings cover the dividend (the inverse of the payout ratio).
notes: Below about 1.5 the dividend may be at risk if profits fall.

name: Tangible Book Value per Share
description: Gives book value per share excluding goodwill and other intangible assets.
notes: Banks are often valued on price to tangible book value.

name: Graham Number
description: Gives Benjamin Graham's upper bound for a defensive investor's purchase price: √(22.5 × EPS × BVPS).
notes: 22.5 = 15 (maximum P/E) × 1.5 (maximum P/B).

name: Altman Z″-Score (Non-Manufacturers and Emerging Markets)
description: Predicts financial distress for non-manufacturing firms (Altman 1995), without the sales-based term.
notes: Above 2.6 safe, 1.1–2.6 grey zone, below 1.1 distress.

name: Beneish M-Score (Earnings Manipulation)
description: Scores the likelihood that a company has manipulated its earnings from eight year-on-year ratios (Beneish 1999).
notes: Scores above −1.78 suggest a likely manipulator; the model flagged Enron before its collapse.

name: Accruals Ratio (Balance-Sheet Quality)
description: Measures how much of earnings is not backed by cash, relative to assets.
notes: High accruals tend to predict weaker future earnings (Sloan 1996).

name: Effective Tax Rate
description: Divides the income tax expense by pre-tax profit.
notes: Differs from the statutory rate because of credits, foreign income and permanent differences.

name: Goodwill on Acquisition
description: Gives goodwill: the price paid in excess of the fair value of identifiable net assets (IFRS 3 / ASC 805).
notes: A negative result is a bargain purchase, recognised as a gain.

name: Percentage-of-Completion Revenue
description: Recognises revenue on a long-term contract in proportion to the costs incurred (input method, IFRS 15).
notes: Subtract revenue recognised in earlier periods for this period's amount.

name: Materials Price Variance
description: Measures the cost effect of paying more (positive, unfavourable) or less than the standard price.
notes: Part of standard-cost variance analysis; the quantity variance covers usage.

name: Materials Quantity Variance
description: Measures the cost effect of using more (unfavourable) or less material than the standard allows for actual output.
notes: Labour efficiency variance uses the same form with hours and the standard wage rate.

name: Target Profit Units
description: Gives the sales volume needed to earn a target profit (cost–volume–profit analysis).
notes: With zero target profit it is the break-even volume.

name: Rule of 40 (SaaS)

variables.label: Profit margin, e.g. FCF or EBITDA (%)

description: Adds revenue growth and profit margin; software companies above 40 % are considered healthy.
notes: Lets fast-growing loss-makers and slower profitable firms be compared on one scale.

name: Burn Multiple
description: Divides net cash burned by net new annual recurring revenue added in the same period (Sacks 2020).
notes: Below 1 is excellent, above 2 suspect.

name: Cash Runway
description: Gives how many months a company can operate before its cash runs out at the current burn rate.
notes: Start-ups usually raise money when about 12–18 months remain.

name: Net Revenue Retention
description: Gives the share of recurring revenue kept from existing customers after a year, including upsells.
notes: Above 100 % means the customer base grows even without new customers.

name: CAC Payback Period
description: Gives the months of gross profit needed to earn back the cost of acquiring a customer.
notes: SaaS companies aim for under 12–18 months.

name: Customer Lifetime Value (Churn-Based)
description: Estimates lifetime gross profit per customer as margin per month divided by the monthly churn rate.
notes: Average customer lifetime is 1/churn months (50 months here).
